title: Sliding Window
tagline: Reuse the previous window's work — answer subarray/substring questions in one pass.

intuition.analogy: Imagine a fixed-width window slid across a long panorama. Instead of re-photographing the whole scene each time you shift, you just see one new strip on the right and lose one strip on the left. The bulk of the view is reused.
paragraphs: Many problems ask about contiguous subarrays or substrings: the maximum sum of k elements, the longest substring without repeats, the smallest window containing all required characters. Recomputing each window from scratch is O(n·k) or worse.

The sliding window keeps a running summary (a sum, a frequency map, a count). When the window moves right, you add the entering element and remove the leaving one — an O(1) update — so the whole sweep is O(n).

Two flavours: fixed-size windows (move both ends together) and variable-size windows (expand the right to include more, shrink the left while a constraint is violated). The variable form is the one interviewers love.
intuition.keyIdea: Maintain an incremental summary of the current window and update it in O(1) as the window slides, instead of recomputing.

steps.title: Initialise the first window
steps.detail: For fixed size k, compute the summary of the first k elements. For variable size, start with an empty window at the left.

steps.title: Slide / expand the right edge
steps.detail: Add the new right element to the summary.

steps.title: Shrink the left edge when needed
steps.detail: Fixed size: drop the element k positions back. Variable size: while the constraint is violated, remove a[left] and advance left.

steps.title: Record the answer
steps.detail: After each valid window, update best (max length, min length, max sum, …).

complexity.timeReason: Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once, so total pointer movement is ≤ 2n.
complexity.spaceReason: Constant for numeric sums; up to O(alphabet/k) for frequency maps.

pitfalls: For variable windows, make sure the shrink loop is a 'while', not an 'if' — multiple elements may need removing.
Off-by-one in window length: it's right - left + 1.
Forgetting to update the summary symmetrically when both adding and removing.

dryRun.clickMoment: Look at the Sum column: every step is one add and one subtract — never a full re-sum of three elements. That O(1) update across n positions is what makes it linear.

problems.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
problems.statement: Find the contiguous subarray of length k with the maximum average.
problems.hint: Fixed-size window sum; slide and track the max.

approach: Fixed-size window of length k: compute the first window's sum, then slide by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one.
Track the max average = max window sum / k. O(n) with O(1) memory.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
problems.hint: Variable window; jump left past the last duplicate position.
problems.tests: Variable window with a last-seen map.

approach: Grow a window [l, r]; track the last index each character appeared. When a repeat is inside the window, jump l past the previous occurrence.
The answer is the maximum window width seen. Each index is visited once, O(n).

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.statement: Smallest length of a subarray with sum ≥ target.
problems.hint: Expand right to grow the sum; shrink left while sum ≥ target.

approach: Expand the right edge adding to a running sum. Whenever sum >= target, shrink from the left while it still holds, recording the minimum window length.
Each index enters and leaves the window once, so it is O(n) despite the nested shrink loop.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.statement: Does s2 contain a permutation of s1 as a substring?
problems.hint: Fixed window of size |s1|; compare frequency counts.

approach: We seek a window of length len(s1) in s2 whose character counts match s1's exactly. Maintain a fixed-size sliding window of frequency counts.
Track how many of the 26 letters currently match the target count; the window is a permutation when all 26 match.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.statement: Smallest window in s containing all characters of t.
problems.hint: Expand to satisfy all required counts, then shrink to minimise while still valid.

approach: Keep a `need` count of t's characters and a `missing` counter. Expand right, decrementing missing when a needed char is covered.
Once missing hits 0, shrink from the left to drop unnecessary characters, recording the smallest valid window. O(n).
